```{python}
# | echo: false
# | output: false
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This deck draws every exhibit from the Marimo notebook (customer-base-audit.py)
#
# How: parse the notebook, strip marimo's scaffolding (the `@app.cell` /
# `def _(...)` wrapper and the cell-level `return`), drop the blocks that exist
# only for the marimo UI (`mo.*`, the `how(...)` explainer callouts), then exec
# the rest here. That yields bar_distribution, decile_report_gt,
# profit_bridge_chart, venn_two, line_chart, second_purchase_chart,
# cohort_lines, the annual bar charts, cohort_flow_chart, the `cba` plotly
# theme, plus YEAR_* / FOCUS_COHORT_* and every lens dataset.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
import ast
import re
import textwrap
from pathlib import Path

_NB = Path("notebooks/analyses/customer-base-audit.py")


def _notebook_source(path: Path) -> str:
    src = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    src = src[: re.search(r"\nif __name__ ==", src).start()]
    out = []
    for cell in re.split(r"(?m)^(?=@app\.cell)", src)[1:]:
        lines = cell.splitlines()
        di = next((i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if re.match(r"def _\(", l)), None)
        if di is None:
            continue
        j = di
        while not lines[j].rstrip().endswith("):"):  # multi-line signatures
            j += 1
        body = lines[j + 1 :]
        # marimo's cell-level return is always last — truncate there
        ri = next(
            (i for i, l in enumerate(body) if re.match(r"^    return(\s|$|\()", l)),
            None,
        )
        if ri is not None:
            body = body[:ri]
        body = textwrap.dedent("\n".join(body))
        if not body.strip():
            continue
        kept = []
        for node in ast.parse(body).body:
            seg = ast.get_source_segment(body, node)
            if seg is None or re.search(r"\bmo\.|\bhow\(", seg):
                continue  # marimo-only UI blocks
            kept.append(seg)
        if kept:
            out.append("\n".join(kept))
    return "\n\n".join(out)


exec(compile(_notebook_source(_NB), str(_NB), "exec"), globals())

# --- exhibit geometry ------------------------------------------------------
# Reveal keeps non-active slides hidden, so a responsive (autosize) plotly
# figure measures a zero-width container at init and only corrects itself after
# a resize event — which is why charts used to need a refresh/zoom to fit.
# Explicit pixel sizes avoid the problem, and on this canvas they are known
# exactly rather than guessed:
#
#   body width = 1180 (canvas) - 2 x 46 (slide padding)          = 1088
#   two equal columns, 26px gutter        -> (1088 - 26) / 2     =  531
#   60/40 split, 26px gutter              -> 1088 x .6 - 15.6    =  637
#   three equal columns, 2 x 26px gutter  -> (1088 - 52) / 3     =  345
#
# the `.body` flex region centres each figure in the height left over after
# the header, takeaway and footer, so the same numbers reproduce the same whitespace.
COL_FULL, COL_HALF, COL_WIDE, COL_THIRD = 1088, 531, 637, 345
COL_GAP = 26  # .columns gutter in slides.scss — keep the two in step


def col_px(pct, n=2, gap=COL_GAP, total=COL_FULL):
    """Rendered width of a `.column width="<pct>%"` in an n-column row.

    A column's `width:<pct>` is only its flex BASIS: the bases sum to the full
    body width, so the row overflows by the gutters and every column shrinks in
    proportion. The gutters therefore come off the total before the split, which
    is why this is not simply `pct% of 1088`. Floored, not rounded: a figure a
    shade narrower than its column is invisible, one a shade wider clips.
    """
    return int(pct / 100 * (total - gap * (n - 1)))


def fit(fig, width, height):
    """Size a notebook figure for the fixed 1180x664 slide canvas."""
    fig.update_layout(autosize=False, width=width, height=height)
    return fig
```

## [Executive summary]{.eyebrow}The average customer describes no one — value is concentrated, and its decay is driven by repeat buying

::::: {.body .top}
<ul class="points">
<li><b>Value is concentrated.</b> A small share of customers accounts for most transactions, spend, and profit — the base is not uniform.</li>
<li><b>The “average customer” describes no one.</b> Every behavioural measure is right-skewed, so the mean sits well above the median and most customers fall below the mean.</li>
<li><b>Cohorts decay through fewer active buyers, not weaker spending.</b> Spend per active customer stays broadly flat; the base shrinks because fewer customers remain — so <b>repeat buying is the lever</b>.</li>
<li><b>Behaviour is stable and predictable</b> once heterogeneity is taken into account — the same patterns recur across periods and cohorts.</li>
</ul>

::: {.takeaway}
Manage the customer base as a portfolio: protect the high-value minority and lift repeat buying, rather than chase an “average” customer that does not exist.
:::
:::::

::: {.footer}
Madrigal transaction sample, 2016–2019
:::

A 1% sample of **Madrigal**'s transaction records — 70,041 customers, aggregated to the quarter, for 16 quarters (Q1 2016 – Q4 2019). Each customer carries transactions, spend, profit, and an acquisition cohort.

The audit is **descriptive**: it summarises how customers behave, it does not forecast.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.note}
[One identity ties it together]{.note-h}

**Profit = N~c~ × AOF × AOV × Margin**

[(active customers × orders per customer × spend per order × profit margin)]{style="color:#6b7280"}

Every result below traces a change in profit to one of these factors — **fewer customers**, **less frequent orders**, **smaller orders**, or **thinner margins**.
:::
:::

## [Implications]{.eyebrow}Four moves follow directly from the audit

::::: {.body .top}
<ul class="points">
<li><b>Treat the base as a portfolio.</b> Segment by value and manage the high-value minority explicitly — the average hides them.</li>
<li><b>Make repeat buying the first lever.</b> Cohort decay is driven by fewer active customers, so small repeat-buying gains compound across every cohort.</li>
<li><b>Win the second purchase early.</b> Repeat behaviour is largely set in the first few quarters — invest in early-life experience.</li>
<li><b>Acquire more of the right customers.</b> Per-customer behaviour is stable, so growth comes mainly from adding customers like the ones you keep.</li>
</ul>

::: {.takeaway}
None of these require an “average customer”. They require managing a heterogeneous base by value and by age.
:::
:::::

## [Appendix · Method]{.eyebrow}A definitions note: keep the two “average transaction” numbers apart

::: {.slide-sub}
“Average spend per transaction” is two different numbers
:::

::::: {.body .top}
::: {.note}
<ul class="points" style="margin-top:8px">
<li><b>AOV — ratio of totals.</b> Total spend ÷ total transactions. A <b>transaction-weighted</b> average, so frequent buyers dominate it.</li>
<li><b>Mean of per-customer averages.</b> Average each customer's own spend-per-transaction, then average across customers — every customer counts equally, so one-and-done-in-2019 buyers pull it up.</li>
</ul>

The two are equal only if every customer transacts the same number of times, which never happens. The gap's direction is informative: here the weighted figure sits below the unweighted one, so heavier buyers have **smaller** baskets than light buyers.

[Convention used throughout: “AOV” always means the transaction-weighted ratio of totals.]{style="color:#6b7280"}
:::
:::::

::: {.footer}
See Lens 1 — Distribution of average spend per transaction
:::

## [Appendix · Method]{.eyebrow}A wording note: “repeat-buying rate” and “% of cohort active”, not “retention”

::::: {.body .top}
::: {.note}
<ul class="points">
<li><b>Why not “retention” here.</b> Madrigal is <b>noncontractual</b> — a customer who skips a period has not necessarily left. “Retention” properly describes contractual renewal / survival, where a cancellation is actually observed.</li>
<li><b>% of cohort active.</b> The share of a cohort that buys in a period — <b>unconditional</b>, and it includes one-time buyers.</li>
<li><b>Repeat-buying rate.</b> The <b>conditional</b> quantity — the share of customers active in one period who buy again in the next.</li>
<li><b>Carryover.</b> For value: a cohort's profit in one year relative to the year before (what the cohort-flow chart annotates).</li>
</ul>

Likewise the two “one-and-done” figures are different: **one-and-done in 2019** (exactly one transaction that year, Lens 1) is not the share of a cohort that **never makes a second purchase** (Lens 3).
:::
:::::

::: {.footer}
After Fader, Hardie & Ross, *The Customer-Base Audit* (2022), Ch. 9 — “Be Wary of the ‘R’ Word”
:::
